Krichene and Rendle show that sampled recommendation metrics can reverse model rankings relative to full-catalog metrics, even in expectation; smaller candidate sets also make top-heavy metrics behave more like AUC. Thus HR@10 against 99 sampled negatives measures success within that candidate protocol and cannot establish full-catalog HR@10 superiority. Keep the pinned evaluator unchanged and describe improvements specifically as sampled-validation gains. Their proposed corrections trade bias against variance; applying them would change this benchmark’s objective. [On Sampled Metrics for Item Recommendation](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/)

For uncertainty analysis, a suitable application of paired bootstrap resampling is to retain each user’s hit indicators for both checkpoints, resample the same user indices for both within each category, and recompute the equally weighted four-category mean difference. With 200 users/category, one additional hit changes category HR by 0.005 and macro HR by 0.00125. Report the difference and its bootstrap interval; pairing captures disagreement between models. This interval is conditional on the fixed candidates and trained checkpoints, excluding negative-sampling and training variability. [Bootstrap comparison methods](https://www.research.ed.ac.uk/en/publications/statistical-significance-tests-for-machine-translation-evaluation/)

Repeatedly choosing the best checkpoint or hypothesis on the same validation users creates selection optimism: a bootstrap interval computed after selection does not remove that bias. Treat small winning margins as provisional, record how many alternatives were evaluated, and avoid interpreting the maximum validation score as an unbiased generalization estimate. Keep test labels inaccessible throughout search. [Cawley and Talbot, model-selection bias](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v11/cawley10a.html)
